en.errors.git.gitDirPermissionDenied.sugges: Open **{system_settings} > {privacy_and_security} > {files_and_folders}** and grant Cmdr access. In Terminal, `ls -la .git` shows the current owner and mode.
en.errors.listing.attributeNotFound.suggest: This file system may not support the metadata Cmdr needs. Try the operation on a different volume, or copy the file to your Mac’s internal drive first.
en.errors.listing.authRequiredEneedauth.sug:
Here’s what to try:
- Disconnect and reconnect the volume in Finder
- Enter your username and password when prompted
- If you’re not sure about the credentials, check with the server’s administrator
en.errors.listing.connectionRefused.explana: The server actively refused the connection. This usually means the server software (for example, an SMB or NFS service) isn’t running, or it’s configured to reject connections from this Mac.
en.errors.listing.connectionRefused.suggest:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the server is running and its file sharing service is active
- Verify the server address and port are correct
- In Terminal, try `ping <hostname>` to check if the server is reachable at all
- Navigate here again to retry
en.errors.listing.connectionReset.suggestio:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the server is running
- In Terminal, try `ping <hostname>` to test if the server is reachable
- Navigate here again to retry
en.errors.listing.connectionTimedOut.sugges:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the device or server is powered on and reachable
- Check your Wi-Fi or Ethernet connection
- In Terminal, try `ping <hostname>` to test if the server is reachable
- Try again
en.errors.listing.connectionTimedOutErrno.s:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the device or server is powered on and reachable
- Check your Wi-Fi or Ethernet connection
- In Terminal, try `ping <hostname>` to test connectivity
- Navigate here again to retry
en.errors.listing.couldntReadUnknown.sugges:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the disk or device is still connected
- Navigate here again to retry
- If this keeps happening, open **Disk Utility** and run **First Aid** on this volume
en.errors.listing.diskFullErrno.suggestion:
Here’s what to try:
- Free up space by moving or deleting files you no longer need
- Empty the Trash (right-click the Trash icon in the Dock)
- In Terminal, run `df -h` to see how much space is left on each volume
- Check **{system_settings} > General > Storage** for a breakdown of what’s using space
en.errors.listing.diskReadProblem.suggestio:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the disk or device is still properly connected
- Open **Disk Utility** (search for it in Spotlight) and run **First Aid** on this volume
- If this keeps happening, back up your data as soon as possible. The disk may be developing bad sectors or starting to wear out.
en.errors.listing.emptyRootICloud.explanati:
Cmdr opened iCloud Drive but it came back with no files. macOS hides iCloud Drive contents from apps that don’t have **{full_disk_access}**, so granting Cmdr that permission is the most likely fix.

If your iCloud Drive really is empty, you can ignore this hint.
en.errors.listing.emptyRootICloud.suggestio:
Here’s what to try:
- Open [**{system_settings} > {privacy_and_security}**](x-apple.systempreferences:com.apple.preference.security?Privacy) and pick **{full_disk_access}**
- Add Cmdr (use the **+** button) and toggle it on
- Quit and reopen Cmdr
- Come back here to retry
en.errors.listing.emptyRootICloud.title: iCloud Drive looks empty
en.errors.listing.hostDown.suggestion:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the host is powered on and connected to the network
- In Terminal, try `ping <hostname>` to test if it’s reachable
- If it’s a NAS or server, check its management interface
- Navigate here again once the host is back
en.errors.listing.hostUnreachable.suggestio:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the host is powered on and on the same network
- If you need a VPN to reach it, make sure the VPN is connected
- In Terminal, try `ping <hostname>` to test connectivity
- Navigate here again once the host is reachable
en.errors.listing.ioSerious.suggestion:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the disk or device is still connected
- Try again
- If this keeps happening, try running **Disk Utility > First Aid** on this volume
en.errors.listing.lockUnavailable.suggestio:
Here’s what to try:
- Close some apps, especially ones that work with many files (editors, IDEs, backup tools)
- In Terminal, run `lsof | wc -l` to see how many files are open across all apps
- If the problem keeps happening, you can raise the limit with `ulimit -n 4096` in Terminal
- Navigate here again to retry
en.errors.listing.nameTooLongErrno.explanat: The file or folder name exceeds the system’s limit (255 characters on most Mac volumes). This can also happen when the full path (all folders combined) exceeds the system’s maximum path length.
en.errors.listing.networkDown.explanation: Your Mac’s network connection is down, so Cmdr can’t reach this volume. This could mean Wi-Fi is disconnected, an Ethernet cable is unplugged, or the network interface is disabled.
en.errors.listing.networkDown.suggestion:
Here’s what to try:
- Check Wi-Fi or Ethernet status in **{system_settings} > Network**
- If you’re on Wi-Fi, try turning it off and on again
- In Terminal, run `ping google.com` to test your connection
- Navigate here again once you’re back online
en.errors.listing.networkUnreachable.sugges:
Here’s what to try:
- Check your Wi-Fi or Ethernet connection
- Make sure you’re on the right network (for example, your office Wi-Fi or VPN)
- In Terminal, try `ping <hostname>` to test if the server is reachable
- Navigate here again once you’re connected
en.errors.listing.noPermissionErrno.explana: Cmdr doesn’t have permission to access `{path}`. macOS controls which apps can access which folders, and Cmdr hasn’t been granted access to this one yet.
en.errors.listing.noPermissionErrno.suggest:
Here’s what to try:
- Open **{system_settings} > {privacy_and_security} > {files_and_folders}** and grant Cmdr access
- Check the folder’s permissions in Finder: right-click it, choose Get Info, and look under Sharing & Permissions
- If this is a shared folder, ask the owner to update permissions
- In Terminal, run `ls -la` on this path to see the current permissions
en.errors.listing.notEnoughMemory.suggestio:
Here’s what to try:
- Close some apps to free up memory, especially ones using lots of resources (browsers with many tabs, editors, media apps)
- Check memory usage in **Activity Monitor** (search for it in Spotlight)
- Navigate here again to retry
en.errors.listing.notFound.suggestion:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the path is spelled correctly
- If this is on a network drive, make sure it’s connected and the share is accessible
- Navigate to the parent folder and look for the item there
- In Terminal, run `ls -la` on the parent folder to see what’s there
en.errors.listing.notPermitted.explanation: macOS blocked Cmdr from accessing `{path}`. This usually means the folder is protected by macOS security policies, or Cmdr hasn’t been granted the right permissions yet.
en.errors.listing.notPermitted.suggestion:
Here’s what to try:
- Open **{system_settings} > {privacy_and_security} > {files_and_folders}** and grant Cmdr access
- If this is a system-protected folder, you may need to grant Cmdr **{full_disk_access}** under {privacy_and_security}
- In Terminal, run `ls -la` on this path to check ownership and permissions
en.errors.listing.notSupported.suggestion: Try a different approach, or use Finder for this operation.
en.errors.listing.notSupportedErrno.suggest: Try a different approach, or use Finder for this operation. If you’re working with an external drive, it might be formatted with a file system that has limitations (for example, FAT32 can’t store files of 4 GiB or more).
en.errors.listing.pathNotFoundErrno.suggest:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the path is spelled correctly
- If this is on a network drive, make sure it’s connected and the share is accessible
- Navigate to the parent folder and look for the item there
- In Terminal, run `ls -la` on the parent folder to see what’s there
en.errors.listing.permissionDenied.explanat: Cmdr doesn’t have permission to access `{path}`. macOS controls which apps can access which folders, and Cmdr hasn’t been granted access to this one yet.
en.errors.listing.permissionDenied.suggesti:
Here’s what to try:
- Open **{system_settings} > {privacy_and_security} > {files_and_folders}** and grant Cmdr access
- Check the folder’s permissions in Finder: right-click the folder, choose Get Info, and look under Sharing & Permissions
- If this is a shared folder, ask the owner to update permissions
- In Terminal, run `ls -la` on the path to see the current permissions
en.errors.listing.quotaExceeded.suggestion:
Here’s what to try:
- Free up space by removing files you no longer need on this volume
- Ask your system administrator to increase your quota
- In Terminal, run `quota` to see your current usage and limit
en.errors.listing.readOnlyVolumeErrno.expla: This volume is mounted as read-only, so Cmdr can’t make changes to it. This could be because the device has a physical write-protection switch, the disk image was mounted read-only, or the file system doesn’t support writing.
en.errors.listing.remotePermissionDenied.ex: `{path}` lives on a network share, and the account you connected with doesn’t have permission to open it. The server turns the request down before macOS is involved, so this isn’t a privacy setting on your Mac.
en.errors.listing.remotePermissionDenied.su:
Here’s what to try:
- Check the folder’s permissions on the server, and which account you mounted the share with
- Some folders belong to the server’s own system account (`lost+found` on a Linux share, for example) and stay closed to everyone else
- To connect as someone else, eject the share and mount it again with those credentials
en.errors.listing.resourceBusy.suggestion: Wait a moment, then navigate here again. If it keeps happening, check which app might be holding the file open (in Terminal, run `lsof +D <folder-path>` to see which processes are using this folder).
en.errors.listing.staleConnection.suggestio:
Here’s what to try:
- Navigate away from this folder and come back
- If this is a network drive, try unmounting and remounting it in Finder
- Check that the server hosting this folder is running
- In Terminal, run `mount` to see currently mounted volumes
en.errors.listing.storageFull.suggestion:
Here’s what to try:
- Free up space by moving or deleting files you no longer need
- Empty the Trash (right-click the Trash icon in the Dock)
- In Terminal, run `df -h` to see how much space is left on each volume
en.errors.listing.symlinkLoopErrno.suggesti:
Here’s what to try:
- In Terminal, run `ls -la` on this path to see where the symbolic links point
- Find and fix the link that creates the loop
- If you’re not sure which link is the problem, follow them one by one with `readlink <path>`
en.errors.listing.tccRestricted.explanation: Cmdr can’t read `{path}` because macOS hasn’t granted access to this folder yet. This is a privacy gate, not a Cmdr bug.
en.errors.listing.tccRestricted.title: This folder is restricted by macOS
en.errors.listing.temporarilyUnavailable.su: Navigate here again to retry. This usually resolves on its own. If it keeps happening, the system might be under heavy load. Check **Activity Monitor** for apps consuming a lot of resources.
Here’s what to try:
- Navigate here again to retry
- If this keeps happening, open **Disk Utility** (search for it in Spotlight) and run **First Aid** on this volume to check for file system problems
en.errors.mount.signInHelperStuck: “{server}” is answering, but macOS’s network sign-in helper looks stuck, so no share can connect right now. To restart it, open Terminal, run killall NetAuthSysAgent, then try again. macOS starts the helper again on its own.
en.errors.mutation.fileLocked: This item is locked. Unlock it in Finder’s Get Info panel, then try again.
en.errors.mutation.parentNotWritable: Cmdr can’t write into “{path}”. Check the folder’s permissions in Finder.
en.errors.mutation.sipProtected: macOS protects this item with System Integrity Protection, so it can’t be renamed.
en.errors.mutation.trashNotSupported: This volume has no Trash, so the only way is to delete permanently.
en.errors.mutation.trashRefused: macOS wouldn’t move this to the Trash.
en.errors.provider.iCloud.needsAction:
This folder is managed by **{name}**. Here’s what to try:
- Check that iCloud Drive is enabled in **{system_settings} > Apple Account > iCloud**
- Make sure you’re signed in to the right Apple account
- Check your iCloud storage isn’t full
en.errors.provider.iCloud.transient:
This folder is managed by **{name}**. Here’s what to try:
- Check your internet connection
- Make sure you’re signed in to iCloud in {system_settings}
- Navigate here again to retry
en.errors.provider.macDroid.needsAction:
This folder is managed by **MacDroid**. Here’s what to try:
- Open MacDroid and check that your phone is connected
- Make sure your phone is unlocked with the screen on
- Check that USB file transfer mode is enabled on your phone
en.errors.provider.macDroid.serious:
This folder is managed by **MacDroid**. Here’s what to try:
- Unplug and replug the USB cable
- Restart MacDroid
- Try a different USB port or cable
en.errors.provider.macDroid.transient:
This folder is managed by **MacDroid**. Here’s what to try:
- Open MacDroid and check that your phone is connected
- Make sure your phone is unlocked and set to file transfer mode
- Unplug and replug the USB cable, then navigate here again
en.errors.provider.macFuse.needsAction:
This is a **macFUSE** mount. Here’s what to try:
- Check that the FUSE process backing this mount is still running
- Force-unmount and remount the volume if needed
- Make sure macFUSE is up to date in **{system_settings} > General > Login Items & Extensions**
en.errors.provider.macFuse.serious:
This is a **macFUSE** mount. The FUSE process backing it has likely crashed or disconnected. Here’s what to try:
- Force-unmount the volume: run `umount -f /Volumes/<name>` in Terminal
- Remount using the original mount command
- If this keeps happening, check that macFUSE is up to date
en.errors.provider.macFuse.transient:
This is a **macFUSE** mount. The remote server may be slow or unreachable. Here’s what to try:
- Check your network connection
- Check that the remote server is running
- Navigate here again to retry
en.errors.provider.pCloudFuse.needsAction:
This folder is on **pCloud**’s virtual drive. Here’s what to try:
- Make sure the pCloud app is running and you’re signed in
- Check your internet connection
- After a macOS update, re-approve pCloud’s system extension in **{system_settings} > General > Login Items & Extensions**
en.errors.provider.pCloudFuse.serious:
This folder is on **pCloud**’s virtual drive. The pCloud FUSE process may have crashed. Here’s what to try:
- Quit and reopen the pCloud app
- If the drive doesn’t reappear, force-unmount it: run `umount -f /Volumes/pCloudDrive` in Terminal
- After a macOS update, re-approve pCloud’s system extension in **{system_settings} > General > Login Items & Extensions**
en.errors.write.cancelled.message.trash: The move to trash operation was canceled.
The device was disconnected during the move to trash.
en.errors.write.fallback.message.trash: Something went wrong while moving to trash.
en.errors.write.fileLocked.suggestion.mac: Unlock it in Finder (Get Info > uncheck Locked) and try again.
en.errors.write.fileLocked.suggestion.other: The file may be protected. Check its permissions (e.g. via chmod or your file manager) and try again.
en.errors.write.homeFolderMove.message.hold: You can’t move {path} because your home folder is in there, and your Mac expects to find it right where it is.
en.errors.write.homeFolderMove.message.isHo: Hey, your home folder lives right where it is. Move it, and your Mac will look for you in the wrong place next time you log in.
en.errors.write.homeFolderMove.suggestion.i: If you want your files somewhere else, go in there, pick what you need, and move that. Your Mac will thank you.
en.errors.write.homeFolderRename.message.ho: You can’t rename {path} because your home folder is in there, and your Mac expects to find it at this exact path.
en.errors.write.homeFolderRename.message.is: Hey, your Mac knows your home folder by this name. Rename it, and it won’t find you next time you log in.
en.errors.write.homeFolderRename.suggestion: If you really need a new name, macOS has a careful way to do it in Users & Groups. It’s not a quick F2, though.
en.errors.write.ioError.message.trash: Couldn’t move the file to trash.
en.errors.write.landingNotRecorded.suggesti: Try again. If it keeps happening, check that your Mac’s disk has free space, then restart Cmdr.
en.errors.write.permissionDenied.message.tr: You don’t have permission to move files to the trash here.
en.errors.write.permissionDenied.suggestion: Check that you have write access to the parent folder. The file may be locked. Unlock it in Finder (Get Info > uncheck Locked) and try again.
Check that you have write access to the parent folder. The file may be protected. Check its permissions (e.g. via chmod or your file manager) and try again.
Changing it needs administrator rights. To give your own account access, select the folder in Finder, choose Get Info, and look under Sharing & Permissions.
Changing it needs administrator rights. To give your own account access, adjust the folder’s permissions (for example with chmod) and try again.
macOS protects this one itself, so administrator rights won’t change it. The item may be locked: select it in Finder, choose Get Info, and uncheck Locked.
The system protects this one itself, so administrator rights won’t change it. The item may carry a protection flag that has to be cleared first.
en.errors.write.sourceNotFound.message.tras: The file or folder you tried to move to trash no longer exists.
en.errors.write.trashNotSupported.title: Trash not supported
en.errors.write.trashRefused.message.locked: macOS won’t move locked items, and that kept {count} of the items you picked where they were.
en.errors.write.trashRefused.message.noTras: macOS couldn’t find a trash for {count} of the items you picked.
en.errors.write.trashRefused.message.notPer: macOS wouldn’t let Cmdr touch {count} of the items you picked.
en.errors.write.trashRefused.message.other: macOS wouldn’t move {count} of the items you picked to the trash.
en.errors.write.trashRefused.message.ownedB: Another account on this Mac owns {count} of the items you picked, and their folder lets only an item’s owner move it.
en.errors.write.trashRefused.message.trashN: The trash on this drive doesn’t let Cmdr put anything in it, so {count} of the items you picked stayed where they were.
en.errors.write.trashRefused.suggestion.fol: To move them, you need permission to change their folder. Finder shows who can in the folder’s Get Info, under Sharing & Permissions.
en.errors.write.trashRefused.suggestion.loc: To move them, unlock them first in Finder: Get Info, then uncheck Locked.
en.errors.write.trashRefused.suggestion.noF: Cmdr also doesn’t have full disk access on this Mac, which is a common cause. The “No full disk access” badge in the title bar takes you to that choice.
en.errors.write.trashRefused.suggestion.noT: Some places have no trash of their own, including cloud folders and most network drives. You can still delete the items permanently with Shift+F8.
en.errors.write.trashRefused.suggestion.not: The items may sit somewhere macOS keeps to itself. Finder can sometimes still move them, since it can ask for your password.
en.errors.write.trashRefused.suggestion.oth: Check the technical details below for what macOS reported.
en.errors.write.trashRefused.suggestion.own: Finder can still move them after asking for an administrator’s password.
en.errors.write.trashRefused.suggestion.tra: This can happen when the trash folder’s permissions change, for example after moving to a new Mac. You can still delete the items permanently with Shift+F8.
en.errors.write.trashRefused.title: Couldn’t move to trash

{path}

en.fileExplorer.navigation.useSavedPassword: Cmdr can reuse the password macOS already saved for “{displayName}”. You’ll see a system prompt asking to allow Keychain access. That’s expected, so click Allow.
en.fileExplorer.network.osMountFallback.enc: Couldn’t directly connect to <shareName>{share}</shareName>, because the server can’t encrypt the connection and Cmdr is set to always require SMB encryption. You are still connected through macOS’s native SMB network connection, which is a lot slower.

Couldn’t directly connect to <shareName>{share}</shareName>, because the share only accepts encrypted connections and the server didn’t agree on a way to encrypt one with Cmdr. You are still connected through macOS’s native SMB network connection, which is a lot slower.
en.fileExplorer.network.osMountFallback.mes: Couldn’t directly connect to <shareName>{share}</shareName>. You are connected, but only via macOS’s native SMB network connection, which is 4x slower for most connections (sometimes 100x) than Cmdr’s direct connection. Click the button below to try again.
en.fileExplorer.network.osMountFallback.neg: Couldn’t directly connect to <shareName>{share}</shareName>, because the server didn’t confirm the security settings it agreed on with Cmdr. A misbehaving server can cause this, and so can someone tampering with the connection. You are still connected through macOS’s native SMB network connection, which is a lot slower.
en.fileExplorer.network.osMountFallback.oth: Couldn’t directly connect to <shareName>{share}</shareName>, because its files live on another server and Cmdr won’t sign in there on its own. You are still connected through macOS’s native SMB network connection, which is a lot slower.
en.fileExplorer.network.osMountFallback.sha: Couldn’t directly connect to <shareName>{share}</shareName>, because the server says it has no share by that name. You are still connected through macOS’s native SMB network connection, which is a lot slower. This one won’t sort itself out: the share may have been renamed or removed on the server, so it’s worth checking there.
en.fileExplorer.network.share.credentialsSt: Credentials stored locally (no system keyring detected)
en.fileExplorer.networkMount.mountingSlow: Still waiting for macOS to connect. You can cancel at any time.
en.fileExplorer.open.didNotOpen: {fileName} didn’t open. macOS couldn’t find the file, or no app opens it.
en.fileExplorer.open.notOnThisMac: Cmdr can’t open this file in another app yet, because it isn’t a regular file on your Mac. Press {viewKey} to view it.

en.onboarding.fdaBadge.tooltip: You don’t have to grant this, but Cmdr works much better with it: searching your whole drive, reading cloud folders, and changing files macOS keeps to itself. Click to look at the choice again.
en.onboarding.stepAi.bannerBody.denied: You chose not to enable full disk access. We respect that. You’ll then shortly get a few permission requests from macOS for Cmdr to access your Desktop, Downloads, and similar folders. Accept or reject these at will. en.onboarding.stepBeta.signup.unreachable: Couldn’t reach the signup server just now, so you’re not on the list yet. Your address is saved on this Mac: hit Save again in a minute, or any time from Settings › Updates & privacy.

en.onboarding.stepFda.con.body: Full disk access is pretty powerful. It lets the app read any file on your Mac. Only grant this if you trust Cmdr. Cmdr uses this right respectfully, and is <sourceLink>source-available</sourceLink> if you feel unsure.
en.onboarding.stepFda.firstAsk.askPermissio: Would you like to give this app full disk access? Here’s what that means:
en.onboarding.stepFda.firstAsk.explain: You see, Cmdr is a file manager, and it needs to access your disk to see all your files. macOS doesn’t automatically grant permission to this.
en.onboarding.stepFda.granted.title: You granted full disk access!
en.onboarding.stepFda.openSettingsFailed: Cmdr couldn’t open {systemSettings}. Open it yourself, go to {privacyAndSecurity}, then {fullDiskAccess}, and turn on Cmdr.
en.onboarding.stepFda.revoked.ifNot: If it wasn’t intentional, consider allowing full disk access again. Here are the pros and cons:
en.onboarding.stepFda.revoked.intro: It looks like you granted full disk access before but then turned it off.
en.onboarding.stepFda.revoked.noAccess: The app currently has no full disk access.
en.onboarding.stepOptional.indexing.benefit: Instant search of your whole drive. Think Spotlight, but even faster.
en.onboarding.stepOptional.mtp.desc: If you enable this, Cmdr can connect to Android phones, Kindles, cameras, some music players, and any other device that supports the protocols called MTP or PTP. The cost is that macOS also wants to connect to these (and it usually fails, which is why you can’t just use Finder to copy photos from Android phones), so Cmdr has to suppress that macOS process while it’s running. When you quit Cmdr, this is politely restored.
en.onboarding.stepOptional.mtp.summary: Lets you connect Android phones and the such, suppresses macOS native handler
en.onboarding.stepOptional.networking.desc: Having this on means you can connect to SMB servers like company network shares, a home NAS, and the like. The only cost is a macOS permission dialog that pops up and asks you to allow “Local Network”, and one for “Accepting incoming connections”. Both dialogs are harmless, but if you don’t know what these are, they might be scary or annoying.

en.settings.advanced.indexPauseFreeSpacePer: Cmdr pauses drive indexing when free space on your startup disk drops below this percent, so the index doesn’t take the room your own files need. Indexing picks up where it left off once free space climbs one point above it. This works whether the “Low disk space warning” is on or off.
en.settings.advanced.logLlmCalls.descriptio: Save every AI request and response to a local folder (llm-logs) for debugging. These files stay on your Mac and include the file names and paths Cmdr sends to your provider.
en.settings.advanced.oldMacosNoticeShown.de: Internal: tracks whether the one-time best-effort notice for a Mac below the supported macOS version has been shown. Hidden from the UI.

en.settings.advanced.showSafeSaveFiles.desc: When apps like TextEdit and Preview save a file, macOS writes the new version alongside it under a temporary name (ending in “.sb-”) and swaps it in. Turn this off to keep those out of the file list.
en.settings.ai.tooltipLocal: Runs a small language model entirely on your device. Maximum privacy: nothing leaves your computer. Works offline. Uses ~2 GB disk space and ~400 MB memory (varies with context size). Requires Apple silicon (M1+) and macOS 14 or later.

en.settings.fileExplorer.tabs.closedTabHist: How many recently closed tabs to keep per pane for “Reopen closed tab” (⌘⇧T). Higher values let you reopen further back in history; lower values free up memory sooner. Only applies to tabs closed in the current session.

en.settings.fileOperations.adbEnabled.descr: Reach the whole filesystem of an Android phone that has USB debugging turned on, which MTP can’t show you. Needs the Android platform tools (the “adb” command) on this Mac. Leaving this on costs nothing if you have no Android tooling installed.
en.settings.fileOperations.mtpEnabled.descr: Detect and connect to Android and other devices over a USB cable for file browsing and transfers. To use this feature on an Android phone, you’ll want to use a USB cable, then on your phone, go to something like Settings > USB Preferences, and set the connection to “File transfer”, “Android Auto”, or similar. (Varies by device.)
en.settings.fileOperations.pasteClipboardAs: What ⌘V does in a folder when the clipboard holds text, an image, or a PDF instead of copied files.
en.settings.fileOperations.skipConfirmation: F5 and F6 copy and move into the other pane right away, and F8 moves to the trash without asking. A bit risky, since one keypress acts at once. Deleting permanently always asks first.
Skip confirmation for copy, move, and trash
en.settings.fileViewer.suppressBinaryWarnin: F3 opens Cmdr’s file viewer, which shows raw bytes (with lossy UTF-8 for non-text content). When you open an image, PDF, archive, or other binary file, the viewer shows a red banner explaining that ⇧Space (Quick Look) or Enter (open in the associated app) is probably what you wanted. Turn this on (or click “Never show this warning again” in the banner) to suppress the warning for good.
en.settings.finderExtension.description: “Open in Cmdr” is always in the menu’s Services section. This moves it up to the top level, on your startup disk. It adds a small process that runs alongside Finder.
en.settings.finderExtension.label: Show at the top of Finder’s right-click menu
en.settings.finderExtension.notInApplicatio: Move Cmdr to your Applications folder to switch this on.
en.settings.finderExtension.notProductionBu: Only a released copy of Cmdr can switch this on. Dev and test builds don’t carry the Finder extension.
en.settings.listing.showHiddenFiles.descrip: Show dotfiles (like .zshrc) and items the system marks as hidden. Applies to both panes.
en.settings.listing.showTags.description: Show colored dots next to names for files and folders that carry macOS Finder tags.
en.settings.mediaIndex.clip.notSupported: Search by description needs a Mac with Apple silicon.
en.settings.mediaIndex.enabled.description: Read the text inside your images so you can search it. Runs on your Mac and never leaves it. Covers local drives for now.
en.settings.mediaIndex.networkVolumes.optIn: Cmdr reads the text inside these photos so you can search it. It runs on your Mac, and the photos never leave your network.
en.settings.mediaIndex.parallelism.descript: How many workers image indexing runs at once. More can be faster, but on Apple silicon the gain flattens out past two, and higher settings back off on their own when your Mac heats up.
en.settings.mediaIndex.privacyNote: This runs entirely on your Mac using Apple’s built-in Vision framework. Your images never leave your computer, and no AI provider or API key is involved.
en.settings.network.directSmbConnection.des: When enabled, Cmdr establishes a direct connection to SMB shares for faster file operations. The system mount stays for Finder and other apps.
en.settings.network.enabled.description: Discover SMB servers on your local network and connect to them. When off, Cmdr can still read and write files on already-mounted shares, but won’t ask macOS for Local Network access.
en.settings.network.permissionIntroPrefix: Cmdr needs {localNetwork} to find SMB servers, list available shares, and connect directly for faster file transfers. The first time you open Network or use
en.settings.network.permissionWithout: Without it, Cmdr can still read and write files on shares that are already mounted, but you can’t discover new servers or use our faster direct connection.
en.settings.network.requireSmbEncryption.de: Cmdr encrypts its connections to SMB shares, even when the server doesn’t ask for it, and doesn’t open a share whose connection can’t encrypt, including one your Mac connected to without encryption. Guest connections can’t be encrypted, so you’ll need to sign in. Connections Cmdr already has open stay as they are until they reconnect.
en.settings.revealHandler.description: When another app runs “Show in Finder”, Cmdr opens that folder with the file under the cursor. Finder stays your default file manager everywhere else.
en.settings.revealHandler.heldByOtherApp: Currently: {app}. Turning this on hands “Show in Finder” to Cmdr.
en.settings.revealHandler.notInApplications: Move Cmdr to your Applications folder to switch this on. From where it runs now, moving or deleting Cmdr would leave every “Show in Finder” click pointing at nothing.
en.settings.revealHandler.notProductionBuil: Only a released copy of Cmdr can switch this on. Dev and test builds come and go, and deleting one would leave every “Show in Finder” click pointing at nothing.
en.settings.revealHandler.uninstallWarning: <lead>Before you uninstall Cmdr, switch this off.</lead> macOS keeps sending “Show in Finder” here, and with Cmdr gone those clicks quietly do nothing.
en.settings.securityLog.enabled.description: Keep a small file on this Mac that notes security-relevant changes and refusals, like cloud AI consent, an installed update, or an app turned away from the MCP server. It holds no file names, contents, or passwords, and it never leaves your Mac.
en.settings.servers.trustedCertificates.des: When macOS doesn’t trust a server’s certificate, Cmdr asks before it trusts it for you, and remembers your answer here. Home servers often make their own.
en.settings.servers.trustedCertificates.emp: Nothing trusted yet. When you connect to a WebDAV server macOS doesn’t trust, Cmdr shows you its certificate’s fingerprint and asks.
en.settings.summary.imageIndexing: Search the text inside your images. Runs on your Mac, and nothing leaves it.
en.settings.updates.crashReports.descriptio: Automatically send a report when Cmdr crashes or runs into a problem in the background. Includes app version, macOS version, and where in the code the problem happened. Never file names or personal data.
en.settings.updates.emailPrivacyNote: Stored only on your Mac. We never send it together with your usage stats, so those can’t be tied back to you. Used only to reach out and to optionally attach to a report you send. To stop getting emails, use the unsubscribe link in any message we send.
en.shortcuts.conflict.reservedByMacOs: {combo} is reserved by macOS ({command}) and won’t reach Cmdr. Pick a different combo.
en.shortcuts.conflict.systemShortcut: {combo} is usually taken by macOS ({label}), so it may never reach Cmdr. You can free it up in System Settings > Keyboard.
en.shortcuts.section.macOsTooltip: macOS handles this shortcut. Cmdr can’t change it.
en.suggestedOps.approve.trash: Move {countText} {count, plural, one {file} other {files}} to Trash
en.suggestedOps.noTrashTooltip: The drive these files are on keeps no Trash, so approving this deletes them for good.
en.suggestedOps.reversible.trash: You can undo this: {count, plural, one {it goes} other {they go}} to the Trash
en.transfer.systemLockedKept: {count, plural, one {{countText} item is locked by macOS, so it stayed where it was.} other {{countText} items are locked by macOS, so they stayed where they were.}}
en.transfer.trash: Moved {countText} {count, plural, one {file} other {files}} to trash
en.ui.menuBar.label: Menu bar
en.ui.toolAsk.openBundle.body: {name} is a bundle, so opening it runs it as a program.
en.ui.toolAsk.openBundle.title: Run this bundle?
en.ui.toolAsk.quit.title: Quit Cmdr?
en.updates.moveToApplicationsDialog.howTo: Quit Cmdr, drag it into your Applications folder, and open it from there. Every update after that arrives on its own.
en.updates.moveToApplicationsDialog.readOnl: A new version is ready, but Cmdr is running from a read-only spot, usually a disk image that’s still mounted. That means updates have nowhere to land.
en.updates.moveToApplicationsDialog.title: Move Cmdr to your Applications folder
en.updates.moveToApplicationsDialog.translo: A new version is ready, but macOS is running Cmdr from a temporary read-only copy of itself. That’s what happens when you open an app straight from where you downloaded it, and it means updates have nowhere to land.
en.updates.status.heldByPolicy: Cmdr {available} is out, but your organization keeps this Mac on {ceiling} or earlier.
en.updates.status.unwritableAdmin: Cmdr {version} is out, but Cmdr can’t install it itself. Download it from getcmdr.com and drag it into Applications.
en.updates.status.unwritableStandard: Cmdr {version} is out, but your account can’t update Cmdr on this Mac.
en.updates.unwritable.adminDetail: {path} belongs to another account. To update, download Cmdr from <website>getcmdr.com</website> and drag it into Applications. macOS will ask for your password.
en.updates.unwritable.standardDetail: Your account can’t update Cmdr on this Mac. Ask your IT team, or whoever manages this Mac, to update it.
en.viewer.binaryWarning.body: This is the raw view of the file. You might want to view the actual <kindName>{category, select, image {image} document {document} other {{ext} file}}</kindName> instead. To do that, close this window and press <quickLookKey></quickLookKey> to open Quick Look, or press <openKey></openKey> (or double-click the file) to open it in the associated app.
en.viewer.copyDialog.confirmBody: Large pastes can slow down other apps. Try search (⌘F) to narrow it down.
en.viewer.copyDialog.refuseBody: That’s larger than the 100 MB clipboard limit. Try search (⌘F) to find what you need, or save the selection as a file.

en-AU.adb.connect.serverUnreachable: The Android tools on this Mac didn’t answer.
en-AU.adb.readiness.noPermissions: This Mac can’t reach your phone over USB. Try another cable or port.
en-AU.ai.cloudConsent.askCmdr.chatsStayLocal: Your Ask Cmdr chats stay on your Mac, in a local database you can open and read.
en-AU.ai.cloudConsent.askCmdr.protectedContent: Some contents stay home whatever anyone asks: SSH keys, cloud and tool credentials, your keychains, browser data, Mail, Messages, Notes, Cmdr’s own data, and any file holding a private key. Their names can still reach your provider.
en-AU.ai.cloudConsent.logsNote: If you turn on “Log AI model calls” in Advanced settings, Cmdr also saves each request and reply to a folder on your Mac. Those call logs stay local, never sent anywhere.
en-AU.ai.local.notInstalled: Not installed. The local model ({modelName}, {modelSize}) runs entirely on your device for maximum privacy. Requires Apple silicon.
en-AU.ai.managed.localOnlyUnsupported: Your organisation allows only on-device AI, and this Mac can’t run it.
en-AU.ai.secretError.genericBody: Check that your system keyring is available, then try again. If it persists, restart the app.
en-AU.ai.secretError.keychainBody: {op, select, save {Open Keychain Access and check the “Cmdr” entry, or delete it and try saving again.} other {Open Keychain Access, find the “Cmdr” entry, grant access, or delete it and re-enter your key.}}
en-AU.ai.secretError.keychainTitle: {op, select, save {Couldn’t save your API key: macOS Keychain denied access} other {Couldn’t read your saved API key: macOS Keychain denied access}}
en-AU.ai.secretError.keyringBody: Unlock your keyring (Passwords / Keyrings app) and try again.
en-AU.ai.secretError.keyringTitle: {op, select, save {Couldn’t save your API key: your system keyring denied access} other {Couldn’t read your saved API key: your system keyring denied access}}
en-AU.ai.secretError.removeKeychainBody: Open Keychain Access, find the “Cmdr” entry, and delete it there.

en-AU.askCmdr.tool.queueMoveLocked.done: Unlocked Locked items for a move
en-AU.askCmdr.tool.queueMoveLocked.tried: Tried to unlock Locked items for a move
en-AU.askCmdr.wake.needsFullDiskAccess: AI features can’t see your folders yet. Click to set up full disk access.

en-AU.commands.appToggleCliCommand.description: Lets you type cmdr and a path in a terminal to open that file or folder in Cmdr
en-AU.commands.downloadsGoToLatest.description: Opens ~/Downloads and selects the most recent file.
en-AU.commands.editUndoTrash.description: Puts back the files you last moved to the Bin

en-AU.commands.editUndoTrash.many: Undo move to Bin of {countText} {count, plural, one {item} other {items}}

en-AU.commands.fileQuickLook.other.label: Preview
en-AU.commands.fileShowInFinder.mac.label: Show in Finder
en-AU.commands.fileShowInFinder.other.label: Show in file manager
en-AU.commands.handler.getInfo.automationOff: Get info needs Cmdr to control Finder, and that’s turned off. Switch on Finder under Cmdr in {systemSettings} > {privacyAndSecurity} > {automation}.
en-AU.commands.handler.getInfo.notReached: Cmdr couldn’t reach Finder to open Get info. Give it another try.
en-AU.commands.handler.openTerminalHere.appMis: {app} isn’t installed any more, so this opened in Terminal.
Your terminal app isn’t installed any more, so this opened in Terminal.
en-AU.commands.resticForgetPassword.descriptio: Removes the saved password of the restic backup you’re in from Keychain, and locks the backup again
en-AU.commands.tagsToggleBlue.description: Adds or removes the blue Finder tag on the selected files
en-AU.commands.tagsToggleGreen.description: Adds or removes the green Finder tag on the selected files
en-AU.commands.tagsToggleGrey.description: Adds or removes the grey Finder tag on the selected files
en-AU.commands.tagsToggleOrange.description: Adds or removes the orange Finder tag on the selected files
en-AU.commands.tagsTogglePurple.description: Adds or removes the purple Finder tag on the selected files
en-AU.commands.tagsToggleRed.description: Adds or removes the red Finder tag on the selected files
en-AU.commands.tagsToggleYellow.description: Adds or removes the yellow Finder tag on the selected files
en-AU.common.downloadsFdaHint: Cmdr needs Full Disk Access to watch your Downloads folder. <settingsLink>Open System Settings</settingsLink>
en-AU.crashReporter.dialog.body.ended: Cmdr quit unexpectedly last time. Here’s a crash report with details that can help fix this.
en-AU.crashReporter.dialog.privacyNote: It includes the app version, macOS version, and which part of the code ran into the problem. No file names or personal data.
en-AU.downloads.fda.message: Cmdr needs Full Disk Access to watch your Downloads folder.
en-AU.errors.eject.unmountRefusedBySystem: macOS is still using something there. Wait a minute, then try again.
en-AU.errors.git.gitDirPermissionDenied.sugges: Open **{system_settings} > {privacy_and_security} > {files_and_folders}** and grant Cmdr access. In Terminal, `ls -la .git` shows the current owner and mode.
en-AU.errors.listing.attributeNotFound.suggest: This file system may not support the metadata Cmdr needs. Try the operation on a different volume, or copy the file to your Mac’s internal drive first.
en-AU.errors.listing.authRequiredEneedauth.sug:
Here’s what to try:
- Disconnect and reconnect the volume in Finder
- Enter your username and password when prompted
- If you’re not sure about the credentials, check with the server’s administrator
en-AU.errors.listing.connectionRefused.explana: The server actively refused the connection. This usually means the server software (for example, an SMB or NFS service) isn’t running, or it’s configured to reject connections from this Mac.
en-AU.errors.listing.connectionRefused.suggest:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the server is running and its file sharing service is active
- Verify the server address and port are correct
- In Terminal, try `ping <hostname>` to check if the server is reachable at all
- Navigate here again to retry
en-AU.errors.listing.connectionReset.suggestio:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the server is running
- In Terminal, try `ping <hostname>` to test if the server is reachable
- Navigate here again to retry
en-AU.errors.listing.connectionTimedOut.sugges:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the device or server is powered on and reachable
- Check your Wi-Fi or Ethernet connection
- In Terminal, try `ping <hostname>` to test if the server is reachable
- Try again
en-AU.errors.listing.connectionTimedOutErrno.s:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the device or server is powered on and reachable
- Check your Wi-Fi or Ethernet connection
- In Terminal, try `ping <hostname>` to test connectivity
- Navigate here again to retry
en-AU.errors.listing.couldntReadUnknown.sugges:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the disk or device is still connected
- Navigate here again to retry
- If this keeps happening, open **Disk Utility** and run **First Aid** on this volume
en-AU.errors.listing.diskFullErrno.suggestion:
Here’s what to try:
- Free up space by moving or deleting files you no longer need
- Empty the Bin (right-click the Bin icon in the Dock)
- In Terminal, run `df -h` to see how much space is left on each volume
- Check **{system_settings} > General > Storage** for a breakdown of what’s using space
en-AU.errors.listing.diskReadProblem.suggestio:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the disk or device is still properly connected
- Open **Disk Utility** (search for it in Spotlight) and run **First Aid** on this volume
- If this keeps happening, back up your data as soon as possible. The disk may be developing bad sectors or starting to wear out.
en-AU.errors.listing.emptyRootICloud.explanati:
Cmdr opened iCloud Drive but it came back with no files. macOS hides iCloud Drive contents from apps that don’t have **{full_disk_access}**, so granting Cmdr that permission is the most likely fix.

If your iCloud Drive really is empty, you can ignore this hint.
en-AU.errors.listing.emptyRootICloud.suggestio:
Here’s what to try:
- Open [**{system_settings} > {privacy_and_security}**](x-apple.systempreferences:com.apple.preference.security?Privacy) and pick **{full_disk_access}**
- Add Cmdr (use the **+** button) and toggle it on
- Quit and reopen Cmdr
- Come back here to retry
en-AU.errors.listing.emptyRootICloud.title: iCloud Drive looks empty
en-AU.errors.listing.hostDown.suggestion:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the host is powered on and connected to the network
- In Terminal, try `ping <hostname>` to test if it’s reachable
- If it’s a NAS or server, check its management interface
- Navigate here again once the host is back
en-AU.errors.listing.hostUnreachable.suggestio:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the host is powered on and on the same network
- If you need a VPN to reach it, make sure the VPN is connected
- In Terminal, try `ping <hostname>` to test connectivity
- Navigate here again once the host is reachable
en-AU.errors.listing.ioSerious.suggestion:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the disk or device is still connected
- Try again
- If this keeps happening, try running **Disk Utility > First Aid** on this volume
en-AU.errors.listing.lockUnavailable.suggestio:
Here’s what to try:
- Close some apps, especially ones that work with many files (editors, IDEs, backup tools)
- In Terminal, run `lsof | wc -l` to see how many files are open across all apps
- If the problem keeps happening, you can raise the limit with `ulimit -n 4096` in Terminal
- Navigate here again to retry
en-AU.errors.listing.nameTooLongErrno.explanat: The file or folder name exceeds the system’s limit (255 characters on most Mac volumes). This can also happen when the full path (all folders combined) exceeds the system’s maximum path length.
en-AU.errors.listing.networkDown.explanation: Your Mac’s network connection is down, so Cmdr can’t reach this volume. This could mean Wi-Fi is disconnected, an Ethernet cable is unplugged, or the network interface is disabled.
en-AU.errors.listing.networkDown.suggestion:
Here’s what to try:
- Check Wi-Fi or Ethernet status in **{system_settings} > Network**
- If you’re on Wi-Fi, try turning it off and on again
- In Terminal, run `ping google.com` to test your connection
- Navigate here again once you’re back online
en-AU.errors.listing.networkUnreachable.sugges:
Here’s what to try:
- Check your Wi-Fi or Ethernet connection
- Make sure you’re on the right network (for example, your office Wi-Fi or VPN)
- In Terminal, try `ping <hostname>` to test if the server is reachable
- Navigate here again once you’re connected
en-AU.errors.listing.noPermissionErrno.explana: Cmdr doesn’t have permission to access `{path}`. macOS controls which apps can access which folders, and Cmdr hasn’t been granted access to this one yet.
en-AU.errors.listing.noPermissionErrno.suggest:
Here’s what to try:
- Open **{system_settings} > {privacy_and_security} > {files_and_folders}** and grant Cmdr access
- Check the folder’s permissions in Finder: right-click it, choose Get Info, and look under Sharing & Permissions
- If this is a shared folder, ask the owner to update permissions
- In Terminal, run `ls -la` on this path to see the current permissions
en-AU.errors.listing.notEnoughMemory.suggestio:
Here’s what to try:
- Close some apps to free up memory, especially ones using lots of resources (browsers with many tabs, editors, media apps)
- Check memory usage in **Activity Monitor** (search for it in Spotlight)
- Navigate here again to retry
en-AU.errors.listing.notFound.suggestion:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the path is spelled correctly
- If this is on a network drive, make sure it’s connected and the share is accessible
- Navigate to the parent folder and look for the item there
- In Terminal, run `ls -la` on the parent folder to see what’s there
en-AU.errors.listing.notPermitted.explanation: macOS blocked Cmdr from accessing `{path}`. This usually means the folder is protected by macOS security policies, or Cmdr hasn’t been granted the right permissions yet.
en-AU.errors.listing.notPermitted.suggestion:
Here’s what to try:
- Open **{system_settings} > {privacy_and_security} > {files_and_folders}** and grant Cmdr access
- If this is a system-protected folder, you may need to grant Cmdr **{full_disk_access}** under {privacy_and_security}
- In Terminal, run `ls -la` on this path to check ownership and permissions
en-AU.errors.listing.notSupported.suggestion: Try a different approach, or use Finder for this operation.
en-AU.errors.listing.notSupportedErrno.suggest: Try a different approach, or use Finder for this operation. If you’re working with an external drive, it might be formatted with a file system that has limitations (for example, FAT32 can’t store files of 4 GiB or more).
en-AU.errors.listing.pathNotFoundErrno.suggest:
Here’s what to try:
- Check that the path is spelled correctly
- If this is on a network drive, make sure it’s connected and the share is accessible
- Navigate to the parent folder and look for the item there
- In Terminal, run `ls -la` on the parent folder to see what’s there
en-AU.errors.listing.permissionDenied.explanat: Cmdr doesn’t have permission to access `{path}`. macOS controls which apps can access which folders, and Cmdr hasn’t been granted access to this one yet.
en-AU.errors.listing.permissionDenied.suggesti:
Here’s what to try:
- Open **{system_settings} > {privacy_and_security} > {files_and_folders}** and grant Cmdr access
- Check the folder’s permissions in Finder: right-click the folder, choose Get Info, and look under Sharing & Permissions
- If this is a shared folder, ask the owner to update permissions
- In Terminal, run `ls -la` on the path to see the current permissions
en-AU.errors.listing.quotaExceeded.suggestion:
Here’s what to try:
- Free up space by removing files you no longer need on this volume
- Ask your system administrator to increase your quota
- In Terminal, run `quota` to see your current usage and limit
en-AU.errors.listing.readOnlyVolumeErrno.expla: This volume is mounted as read-only, so Cmdr can’t make changes to it. This could be because the device has a physical write-protection switch, the disk image was mounted read-only, or the file system doesn’t support writing.
en-AU.errors.listing.remotePermissionDenied.ex: `{path}` lives on a network share, and the account you connected with doesn’t have permission to open it. The server turns the request down before macOS is involved, so this isn’t a privacy setting on your Mac.
en-AU.errors.listing.remotePermissionDenied.su:
Here’s what to try:
- Check the folder’s permissions on the server, and which account you mounted the share with
- Some folders belong to the server’s own system account (`lost+found` on a Linux share, for example) and stay closed to everyone else
- To connect as someone else, eject the share and mount it again with those credentials
en-AU.errors.listing.resourceBusy.suggestion: Wait a moment, then navigate here again. If it keeps happening, check which app might be holding the file open (in Terminal, run `lsof +D <folder-path>` to see which processes are using this folder).
en-AU.errors.listing.staleConnection.suggestio:
Here’s what to try:
- Navigate away from this folder and come back
- If this is a network drive, try unmounting and remounting it in Finder
- Check that the server hosting this folder is running
- In Terminal, run `mount` to see currently mounted volumes
en-AU.errors.listing.storageFull.suggestion:
Here’s what to try:
- Free up space by moving or deleting files you no longer need
- Empty the Bin (right-click the Bin icon in the Dock)
- In Terminal, run `df -h` to see how much space is left on each volume
en-AU.errors.listing.symlinkLoopErrno.suggesti:
Here’s what to try:
- In Terminal, run `ls -la` on this path to see where the symbolic links point
- Find and fix the link that creates the loop
- If you’re not sure which link is the problem, follow them one by one with `readlink <path>`
en-AU.errors.listing.tccRestricted.explanation: Cmdr can’t read `{path}` because macOS hasn’t granted access to this folder yet. This is a privacy gate, not a Cmdr bug.
en-AU.errors.listing.tccRestricted.title: This folder is restricted by macOS
en-AU.errors.listing.temporarilyUnavailable.su: Navigate here again to retry. This usually resolves on its own. If it keeps happening, the system might be under heavy load. Check **Activity Monitor** for apps consuming a lot of resources.
Here’s what to try:
- Navigate here again to retry
- If this keeps happening, open **Disk Utility** (search for it in Spotlight) and run **First Aid** on this volume to check for file system problems
en-AU.errors.mount.signInHelperStuck: “{server}” is answering, but macOS’s network sign-in helper looks stuck, so no share can connect right now. To restart it, open Terminal, run killall NetAuthSysAgent, then try again. macOS starts the helper again on its own.
en-AU.errors.mutation.fileLocked: This item is locked. Unlock it in Finder’s Get Info panel, then try again.
en-AU.errors.mutation.parentNotWritable: Cmdr can’t write into “{path}”. Check the folder’s permissions in Finder.
en-AU.errors.mutation.sipProtected: macOS protects this item with System Integrity Protection, so it can’t be renamed.
en-AU.errors.mutation.trashNotSupported: This volume has no Bin, so the only way is to delete permanently.
en-AU.errors.mutation.trashRefused: macOS wouldn’t move this to the Bin.
en-AU.errors.provider.iCloud.needsAction:
This folder is managed by **{name}**. Here’s what to try:
- Check that iCloud Drive is enabled in **{system_settings} > Apple Account > iCloud**
- Make sure you’re signed in to the right Apple account
- Check your iCloud storage isn’t full
en-AU.errors.provider.iCloud.transient:
This folder is managed by **{name}**. Here’s what to try:
- Check your internet connection
- Make sure you’re signed in to iCloud in {system_settings}
- Navigate here again to retry
en-AU.errors.provider.macDroid.needsAction:
This folder is managed by **MacDroid**. Here’s what to try:
- Open MacDroid and check that your phone is connected
- Make sure your phone is unlocked with the screen on
- Check that USB file transfer mode is enabled on your phone
en-AU.errors.provider.macDroid.serious:
This folder is managed by **MacDroid**. Here’s what to try:
- Unplug and replug the USB cable
- Restart MacDroid
- Try a different USB port or cable
en-AU.errors.provider.macDroid.transient:
This folder is managed by **MacDroid**. Here’s what to try:
- Open MacDroid and check that your phone is connected
- Make sure your phone is unlocked and set to file transfer mode
- Unplug and replug the USB cable, then navigate here again
en-AU.errors.provider.macFuse.needsAction:
This is a **macFUSE** mount. Here’s what to try:
- Check that the FUSE process backing this mount is still running
- Force-unmount and remount the volume if needed
- Make sure macFUSE is up to date in **{system_settings} > General > Login Items & Extensions**
en-AU.errors.provider.macFuse.serious:
This is a **macFUSE** mount. The FUSE process backing it has likely crashed or disconnected. Here’s what to try:
- Force-unmount the volume: run `umount -f /Volumes/<name>` in Terminal
- Remount using the original mount command
- If this keeps happening, check that macFUSE is up to date
en-AU.errors.provider.macFuse.transient:
This is a **macFUSE** mount. The remote server may be slow or unreachable. Here’s what to try:
- Check your network connection
- Check that the remote server is running
- Navigate here again to retry
en-AU.errors.provider.pCloudFuse.needsAction:
This folder is on **pCloud**’s virtual drive. Here’s what to try:
- Make sure the pCloud app is running and you’re signed in
- Check your internet connection
- After a macOS update, re-approve pCloud’s system extension in **{system_settings} > General > Login Items & Extensions**
en-AU.errors.provider.pCloudFuse.serious:
This folder is on **pCloud**’s virtual drive. The pCloud FUSE process may have crashed. Here’s what to try:
- Quit and reopen the pCloud app
- If the drive doesn’t reappear, force-unmount it: run `umount -f /Volumes/pCloudDrive` in Terminal
- After a macOS update, re-approve pCloud’s system extension in **{system_settings} > General > Login Items & Extensions**

Drop your email and I’ll reach out with the occasional question or update.
The email address you enter here is stored only on your Mac and it’s never connected to your usage stats, the two are intentionally two separate subsystems.
en-AU.onboarding.stepBeta.signup.unreachable: Couldn’t reach the signup server just now, so you’re not on the list yet. Your address is saved on this Mac: hit Save again in a minute, or any time from Settings › Updates & privacy.
en-AU.onboarding.stepFda.alreadyGranted.body: You can revoke it any time in {systemSettings}.
en-AU.onboarding.stepFda.alreadyGranted.title: Cmdr currently has full disk access
en-AU.onboarding.stepFda.con.body: Full disk access is pretty powerful. It lets the app read any file on your Mac. Only grant this if you trust Cmdr. Cmdr uses this right respectfully, and is <sourceLink>source-available</sourceLink> if you feel unsure.
en-AU.onboarding.stepFda.firstAsk.askPermissio: Would you like to give this app full disk access? Here’s what that means:
en-AU.onboarding.stepFda.firstAsk.explain: You see, Cmdr is a file manager, and it needs to access your disk to see all your files. macOS doesn’t automatically grant permission to this.
en-AU.onboarding.stepFda.granted.title: You granted full disk access!
en-AU.onboarding.stepFda.openSettingsFailed: Cmdr couldn’t open {systemSettings}. Open it yourself, go to {privacyAndSecurity}, then {fullDiskAccess}, and turn on Cmdr.
en-AU.onboarding.stepFda.revoked.ifNot: If it wasn’t intentional, consider allowing full disk access again. Here are the pros and cons:
en-AU.onboarding.stepFda.revoked.intro: It looks like you granted full disk access before but then turned it off.
en-AU.onboarding.stepFda.revoked.noAccess: The app currently has no full disk access.
en-AU.onboarding.stepOptional.indexing.benefit: Instant search of your whole drive. Think Spotlight, but even faster.
en-AU.onboarding.stepOptional.mtp.desc: If you enable this, Cmdr can connect to Android phones, Kindles, cameras, some music players, and any other device that supports the protocols called MTP or PTP. The cost is that macOS also wants to connect to these (and it usually fails, which is why you can’t just use Finder to copy photos from Android phones), so Cmdr has to suppress that macOS process while it’s running. When you quit Cmdr, this is politely restored.
en-AU.onboarding.stepOptional.mtp.summary: Lets you connect Android phones and the such, suppresses macOS native handler
en-AU.onboarding.stepOptional.networking.desc: Having this on means you can connect to SMB servers like company network shares, a home NAS, and the like. The only cost is a macOS permission dialog that pops up and asks you to allow “Local Network”, and one for “Accepting incoming connections”. Both dialogs are harmless, but if you don’t know what these are, they might be scary or annoying.
en-AU.operationLog.rollback.interruptedNotice: Cmdr quit before this operation finished, so it may not have recorded everything the operation did. Rolling back reaches only what it recorded.
en-AU.operationLog.skipReason.locked: This is locked so that only an administrator can remove it, so Cmdr left it.

en-AU.queryUi.empty.tipAi: Tip: <newKey>⌘N</newKey> starts fresh, <historyKey>⌘H</historyKey> shows recent searches, <aiKey>⌘Enter</aiKey> runs an AI search.

en-AU.servers.hub.emptyMessage: Add one below, or turn on a Mac or NAS on your network and Cmdr will find it.
en-AU.servers.refusal.certificateUntrusted: macOS doesn’t trust this server’s certificate. Add it in Keychain Access, then try again.
en-AU.servers.refusal.clockSkewed: This Mac’s clock is off by more than 15 minutes, so the server won’t accept Cmdr’s requests. Set the date and time automatically in System Settings, then try again.
en-AU.servers.refusal.exportRefused: {host} doesn’t let this Mac open that export. Check which computers the export allows in the server’s NFS settings.
en-AU.servers.refusal.hostKeyRevoked: The key for {host} is marked as compromised in your SSH settings on this Mac. Cmdr won’t connect to it.
en-AU.servers.refusal.localNetworkHint: If the server is on, check that Cmdr is allowed under {localNetwork}.
en-AU.servers.refusal.s3SavedSecretNotUpdated: Cmdr saved your changes but couldn’t update the secret access key in your Keychain. Save again to try once more.
en-AU.servers.refusal.s3SecretNotMoved: Cmdr couldn’t take the saved secret access key along to the new endpoint, so nothing changed. Check that your Keychain is unlocked, then save again.
en-AU.servers.refusal.s3SecretNotStored: Cmdr couldn’t store this secret access key in your Keychain. Try again, or turn off “Remember in Keychain” to sign in without storing it.
en-AU.servers.refusal.savedSecretNotUpdated: Cmdr saved your changes but couldn’t update the password in your Keychain. Save again to try once more.
en-AU.servers.refusal.secretNotMoved: Cmdr couldn’t take the saved password along to the new address, so nothing changed. Check that your Keychain is unlocked, then save again.
en-AU.servers.refusal.secretNotStored: Cmdr couldn’t store this password in your Keychain. Try again, or turn off “Remember in Keychain” to sign in without storing it.
en-AU.servers.refusal.shareEjectRefused: Cmdr couldn’t eject {name}, so nothing was saved. {reason}
en-AU.servers.refusal.shareMounted: The share {name} is still mounted from the old address. Eject it, then save again.
en-AU.servers.refusal.signInHelperStuck: {host} is answering, but macOS’s network sign-in helper looks stuck. To restart it, open Terminal, run killall NetAuthSysAgent, then try again. macOS starts the helper again on its own.
en-AU.servers.sheet.ejectAndSaveHelp: Cmdr ejects every share still mounted from the old address, then saves the new one.
en-AU.servers.sheet.needsStoredSecret: Reconnecting on its own needs a remembered password. Turn on “Remember in Keychain” and sign in once.
en-AU.servers.sheet.nfsExportsNone: {host} lists no exports for this Mac. Type the export’s path if you know it.
en-AU.servers.sheet.nfsIdentityThisMac: Your IDs on this Mac. Change them if the files on the server belong to someone else.
en-AU.servers.sheet.secretKeptPlaceholder: Saved in Keychain. Leave empty to keep it.
en-AU.settings.advanced.indexPauseFreeSpacePer: Cmdr pauses drive indexing when free space on your startup disk drops below this per cent, so the index doesn’t take the room your own files need. Indexing picks up where it left off once free space climbs one point above it. This works whether the “Low disk space warning” is on or off.
en-AU.settings.advanced.logLlmCalls.descriptio: Save every AI request and response to a local folder (llm-logs) for debugging. These files stay on your Mac and include the file names and paths Cmdr sends to your provider.
en-AU.settings.advanced.oldMacosNoticeShown.de: Internal: tracks whether the one-time best-effort notice for a Mac below the supported macOS version has been shown. Hidden from the UI.
Timeout for resolving network services via Bonjour.
en-AU.settings.advanced.showSafeSaveFiles.desc: When apps like TextEdit and Preview save a file, macOS writes the new version alongside it under a temporary name (ending in “.sb-”) and swaps it in. Turn this off to keep those out of the file list.
en-AU.settings.ai.tooltipLocal: Runs a small language model entirely on your device. Maximum privacy: nothing leaves your computer. Works offline. Uses ~2 GB disk space and ~400 MB memory (varies with context size). Requires Apple silicon (M1+) and macOS 14 or later.
en-AU.settings.ai.tooltipLocalDisabled: Local AI requires Apple silicon (M1 or later). Use Cloud AI instead.
en-AU.settings.appearance.appColor.description: To change your system theme colour, go to System Settings > Appearance.
en-AU.settings.appearance.language.description: Choose the language Cmdr uses. “System default” follows your Mac’s language.
en-AU.settings.appearance.textSize.description: Scales text and UI throughout the app. Compounds with the macOS Accessibility text size, where 100% means “exactly the system size”.
en-AU.settings.appearance.themeColorSwatchAria: Open System Settings to change the system theme colour
en-AU.settings.archives.bundle.description: What pressing Enter does on a .app, .bundle, or .framework.

en-AU.settings.behavior.fileSystemWatching.glo: Press ⌃⌥⌘J from any app to jump to your most recent download. Requires Full Disk Access.
en-AU.settings.behavior.fileSystemWatching.low: How to warn you when your startup disk runs low on free space.
Warn when free space drops below this per cent of your startup disk.

en-AU.settings.behavior.finderExtensionNudgeOf: When the one-time offer to add “Open in Cmdr” to Finder’s right-click menu was made.
Finder menu item offer made at
en-AU.settings.behavior.openTerminalHereApp.de: Cmdr lists the terminal apps it finds on this Mac. To use one it doesn’t know, pick “Choose an app…”.
en-AU.settings.behavior.revealActivationNotice: When Cmdr is set to catch “Show in Finder”, the first one that lands here comes with a note saying why a pane opened instead of Finder. Turn this off to see the note once more.
en-AU.settings.behavior.revealHandler.keywords: show in finder, find in finder, reveal, reveal in finder, default file manager, browser, downloads

en-AU.settings.behavior.textEditorApp.descript: Cmdr lists the text editors macOS knows about on this Mac. To use a different app, pick “Choose an app…”.
en-AU.settings.dataWipe.description: Delete everything Cmdr keeps on this Mac: settings, saved passwords, histories, indexes, and downloaded models. Cmdr quits afterwards.
en-AU.settings.dataWipe.doneMessage: Everything Cmdr kept on this Mac is gone. To remove the app as well, move it to the Bin after Cmdr quits.
en-AU.settings.dataWipe.goes.license: The licence on this Mac. To activate it again, enter the licence key from your purchase email.
en-AU.settings.dataWipe.goes.licenseIfAny: The licence on this Mac, if you activated one. To activate it again, enter the licence key from your purchase email.
en-AU.settings.dataWipe.intro: Cmdr deletes everything it keeps on this Mac, then quits. This can’t be undone.
en-AU.settings.dataWipe.introWithSize: Cmdr deletes everything it keeps on this Mac ({sizeText}), then quits. This can’t be undone.
en-AU.settings.dataWipe.leftover.secretItems: {count, plural, one {One item in Keychain Access named “{itemName}”} other {{countText} items in Keychain Access named “{itemName}”}}
en-AU.settings.dataWipe.leftover.secretsUnread: Any items in Keychain Access named “{itemName}”
en-AU.settings.dataWipe.title: Delete all Cmdr data on this Mac?
en-AU.settings.fileExplorer.suppressQuickLookH: Cmdr uses Space to toggle file selection and ⇧Space for Quick Look (Finder uses plain Space for Quick Look). Each time you press Space in the file list, Cmdr shows a one-paragraph reminder of this difference. Turn this on (or click “Don’t show again” in the toast) to suppress the reminder for good.
Suppress the Space-key Quick Look hint
en-AU.settings.fileExplorer.tabs.closedTabHist: How many recently closed tabs to keep per pane for “Reopen closed tab” (⌘⇧T). Higher values let you reopen further back in history; lower values free up memory sooner. Only applies to tabs closed in the current session.
en-AU.settings.fileOperations.adbBinaryPath.de: Leave this empty and Cmdr looks for adb the usual way, including the Android SDK and Homebrew. Point it somewhere else if you keep the platform tools in their own place.
en-AU.settings.fileOperations.adbEnabled.descr: Reach the whole filesystem of an Android phone that has USB debugging turned on, which MTP can’t show you. Needs the Android platform tools (the “adb” command) on this Mac. Leaving this on costs nothing if you have no Android tooling installed.
en-AU.settings.fileOperations.mtpEnabled.descr: Detect and connect to Android and other devices over a USB cable for file browsing and transfers. To use this feature on an Android phone, you’ll want to use a USB cable, then on your phone, go to something like Settings > USB Preferences, and set the connection to “File transfer”, “Android Auto”, or similar. (Varies by device.)
en-AU.settings.fileOperations.pasteClipboardAs: What ⌘V does in a folder when the clipboard holds text, an image, or a PDF instead of copied files.
en-AU.settings.fileOperations.skipConfirmation: F5 and F6 copy and move into the other pane right away, and F8 moves to the Bin without asking. A bit risky, since one keypress acts at once. Deleting permanently always asks first.
Skip confirmation for copy, move, and bin
en-AU.settings.fileViewer.suppressBinaryWarnin: F3 opens Cmdr’s file viewer, which shows raw bytes (with lossy UTF-8 for non-text content). When you open an image, PDF, archive, or other binary file, the viewer shows a red banner explaining that ⇧Space (Quick Look) or Enter (open in the associated app) is probably what you wanted. Turn this on (or click “Never show this warning again” in the banner) to suppress the warning for good.
en-AU.settings.finderExtension.description: “Open in Cmdr” is always in the menu’s Services section. This moves it up to the top level, on your startup disk. It adds a small process that runs alongside Finder.
en-AU.settings.finderExtension.label: Show at the top of Finder’s right-click menu
en-AU.settings.finderExtension.notInApplicatio: Move Cmdr to your Applications folder to switch this on.
en-AU.settings.finderExtension.notProductionBu: Only a released copy of Cmdr can switch this on. Dev and test builds don’t carry the Finder extension.
en-AU.settings.listing.showHiddenFiles.descrip: Show dotfiles (like .zshrc) and items the system marks as hidden. Applies to both panes.
en-AU.settings.listing.showTags.description: Show coloured dots next to names for files and folders that carry macOS Finder tags.
en-AU.settings.mediaIndex.clip.notSupported: Search by description needs a Mac with Apple silicon.
en-AU.settings.mediaIndex.enabled.description: Read the text inside your images so you can search it. Runs on your Mac and never leaves it. Covers local drives for now.
en-AU.settings.mediaIndex.networkVolumes.optIn: Cmdr reads the text inside these photos so you can search it. It runs on your Mac, and the photos never leave your network.
en-AU.settings.mediaIndex.parallelism.descript: How many workers image indexing runs at once. More can be faster, but on Apple silicon the gain flattens out past two, and higher settings back off on their own when your Mac heats up.
en-AU.settings.mediaIndex.privacyNote: This runs entirely on your Mac using Apple’s built-in Vision framework. Your images never leave your computer, and no AI provider or API key is involved.
en-AU.settings.network.directSmbConnection.des: When enabled, Cmdr establishes a direct connection to SMB shares for faster file operations. The system mount stays for Finder and other apps.
en-AU.settings.network.enabled.description: Discover SMB servers on your local network and connect to them. When off, Cmdr can still read and write files on already-mounted shares, but won’t ask macOS for Local Network access.
en-AU.settings.network.permissionIntroPrefix: Cmdr needs {localNetwork} to find SMB servers, list available shares, and connect directly for faster file transfers. The first time you open Network or use
en-AU.settings.network.permissionWithout: Without it, Cmdr can still read and write files on shares that are already mounted, but you can’t discover new servers or use our faster direct connection.
en-AU.settings.network.requireSmbEncryption.de: Cmdr encrypts its connections to SMB shares, even when the server doesn’t ask for it, and doesn’t open a share whose connection can’t encrypt, including one your Mac connected to without encryption. Guest connections can’t be encrypted, so you’ll need to sign in. Connections Cmdr already has open stay as they are until they reconnect.
en-AU.settings.revealHandler.description: When another app runs “Show in Finder”, Cmdr opens that folder with the file under the cursor. Finder stays your default file manager everywhere else.
en-AU.settings.revealHandler.heldByOtherApp: Currently: {app}. Turning this on hands “Show in Finder” to Cmdr.
en-AU.settings.revealHandler.notInApplications: Move Cmdr to your Applications folder to switch this on. From where it runs now, moving or deleting Cmdr would leave every “Show in Finder” click pointing at nothing.
en-AU.settings.revealHandler.notProductionBuil: Only a released copy of Cmdr can switch this on. Dev and test builds come and go, and deleting one would leave every “Show in Finder” click pointing at nothing.
en-AU.settings.revealHandler.uninstallWarning: <lead>Before you uninstall Cmdr, switch this off.</lead> macOS keeps sending “Show in Finder” here, and with Cmdr gone those clicks quietly do nothing.
en-AU.settings.securityLog.enabled.description: Keep a small file on this Mac that notes security-relevant changes and refusals, like cloud AI consent, an installed update, or an app turned away from the MCP server. It holds no file names, contents, or passwords, and it never leaves your Mac.
en-AU.settings.servers.trustedCertificates.des: When macOS doesn’t trust a server’s certificate, Cmdr asks before it trusts it for you, and remembers your answer here. Home servers often make their own.
en-AU.settings.servers.trustedCertificates.emp: Nothing trusted yet. When you connect to a WebDAV server macOS doesn’t trust, Cmdr shows you its certificate’s fingerprint and asks.
en-AU.settings.summary.imageIndexing: Search the text inside your images. Runs on your Mac, and nothing leaves it.
en-AU.settings.updates.crashReports.descriptio: Automatically send a report when Cmdr crashes or runs into a problem in the background. Includes app version, macOS version, and where in the code the problem happened. Never file names or personal data.
en-AU.settings.updates.emailPrivacyNote: Stored only on your Mac. We never send it together with your usage stats, so those can’t be tied back to you. Used only to reach out and to optionally attach to a report you send. To stop getting emails, use the unsubscribe link in any message we send.
en-AU.shortcuts.conflict.reservedByMacOs: {combo} is reserved by macOS ({command}) and won’t reach Cmdr. Pick a different combo.
en-AU.shortcuts.conflict.systemShortcut: {combo} is usually taken by macOS ({label}), so it may never reach Cmdr. You can free it up in System Settings > Keyboard.
en-AU.shortcuts.section.macOsTooltip: macOS handles this shortcut. Cmdr can’t change it.

en-AU.updates.moveToApplicationsDialog.howTo: Quit Cmdr, drag it into your Applications folder, and open it from there. Every update after that arrives on its own.
en-AU.updates.moveToApplicationsDialog.readOnl: A new version is ready, but Cmdr is running from a read-only spot, usually a disk image that’s still mounted. That means updates have nowhere to land.
en-AU.updates.moveToApplicationsDialog.title: Move Cmdr to your Applications folder
en-AU.updates.moveToApplicationsDialog.translo: A new version is ready, but macOS is running Cmdr from a temporary read-only copy of itself. That’s what happens when you open an app straight from where you downloaded it, and it means updates have nowhere to land.

en-GB.ai.cloudConsent.askCmdr.chatsStayLocal: Your Ask Cmdr chats stay on your Mac, in a local database you can open and read.
en-GB.ai.cloudConsent.askCmdr.protectedContent: Some contents stay home whatever anyone asks: SSH keys, cloud and tool credentials, your keychains, browser data, Mail, Messages, Notes, Cmdr’s own data, and any file holding a private key. Their names can still reach your provider.
en-GB.ai.cloudConsent.logsNote: If you turn on “Log AI model calls” in Advanced settings, Cmdr also saves each request and reply to a folder on your Mac. Those call logs stay local, never sent anywhere.
